cases.title: Movin' Molecules
cases.client: Rook, lead programmer at Pixel Pond Studios
cases.pitch: Pixel Pond Studios is building a video game where water freezes, melts, and boils. Rook needs the water to behave like real science. Scientists measured how fast water molecules move at different temperatures. Build the graph from their data, then use it to help Rook program the physics.
cases.win: Rook's water physics are ready. Players will never know how much science is hiding in that puddle!

cases.title: The Cold Pack Challenge
cases.pitch: Coach Rivera needs instant cold packs for the team's first-aid kit. You'll test four substances by dissolving each one in water and measuring the temperature. Plan a fair test, run it, and recommend the best one. The pack has to get cold fast, stay cold, and not blow the budget.
cases.win: Coach Rivera ordered a case of cold packs, and they're the right ones. Twisted ankles everywhere thank you.

cases.title: Mission to Kestrel-b
cases.client: Captain Juno Park, probe mission planner
cases.pitch: Captain Park is landing a probe on Kestrel-b, a moon with a thick atmosphere where the pressure changes from place to place. The probe needs liquid water to run its experiments. Use the phase diagram for water to pick safe landing sites.
cases.win: The probe touched down right next to liquid water. Mission control is cheering!

cases.title: Fog for Frankenstein
cases.client: Mack, effects designer at the Lantern Light Theater
cases.pitch: The Lantern Light Theater is staging Frankenstein, and the graveyard scene needs creepy fog. Mack uses dry ice, which is solid carbon dioxide. Before the show, Mack needs to understand CO2's phase diagram. Careful: the pressure axis on this one is a stretchy log scale!
cases.win: The graveyard scene is gloriously foggy. (Fun fact: the fog you see is tiny water droplets. The CO2 gas itself is invisible!)

cases.title: The Winter Bounce Test
cases.client: Priya, product tester at Rebound Sports Co.
cases.pitch: Rebound Sports Co. is making basketballs for an outdoor winter league. Priya tested the same ball at different temperatures and recorded the air pressure inside and how high it bounced. Use her table and graph to explain what the air particles are doing.
cases.win: Priya's report is done, and the winter league now keeps its balls warm between games. Science wins again.

cases.title: The Mystery Sample
cases.pitch: A patient's tissue sample came back unlabeled. Dr. Okafor needs a lab with a microscope to compare cell structures and figure out what kind of tissue it is.

cases.title: The Greenhouse Gamble
cases.client: Rosa, owner of Sunny Acres Greenhouse
cases.pitch: Rosa's seedlings are growing at very different rates. She wants to know which factors really matter: light, water, or fertilizer. Plan a fair test to find out.

cases.title: The Wrist Brace Redesign
cases.pitch: A clinic needs a new wrist brace material that's strong, light, and comfortable. Test the options against the clinic's criteria and constraints, then recommend one.

visuals.label: Graph
visuals.title: Speed of Water Molecules at Different Temperatures

questions.prompt: Rook wants the water to glow blue when its molecules reach 650 m/s. The scientists never measured 650 m/s, so use the line. At what temperature does that happen?
questions.why: Find 650 m/s on the y-axis, go straight across to the line, then straight down: 20°C. There's no dot there. The line shows values between the measurements.

questions.prompt: Rook's desert level is 80°C, but the scientists never measured 80°C. Based on the line, about how fast are the molecules moving at 80°C?
questions.why: Go straight up from 80°C to the line. It crosses a little above halfway between the 700 and 750 gridlines: about 725 m/s.

questions.prompt: Rook needs one rule for the game engine. Which statement best describes the overall trend?
questions.why: From the first point to the last, the line keeps rising: hotter water, faster molecules.

questions.prompt: Rook wants to know where heating makes the biggest difference. Pick the TWO sections where the line is steepest, where speed rises fastest for each degree of warming.
questions.why: From -20 to 0°C, speed rose 50 m/s over 20 degrees. From 0 to 40°C, it rose 100 m/s over 40 degrees. Both are 2.5 m/s for every degree, the same steepness. After 40°C the line flattens out.

questions.prompt: Rook wants a bonus level with superheated steam at 140°C. Based on the pattern, what is the best prediction?
questions.why: The speed keeps rising, but the line flattens near the end, so expect a little faster than 750 m/s.

questions.prompt: Rook wants the in-game science tips to be accurate. Pick the TWO statements supported by the graph AND by science.
questions.why: Hotter water has more average kinetic energy, and even ice at -20°C has molecules moving at 550 m/s.

questions.prompt: A coworker claims: "Heating water makes its molecules speed up." Select ALL the statements that are evidence for this claim.
questions.why: Evidence must be true AND show that heating led to more speed. The water being a liquid is true but doesn't show speed changing.

questions.prompt: Rook's next level is at the bottom of a deep ocean, where the pressure is very high. Can THIS graph tell Rook whether the water there is a solid, liquid, or gas?
questions.why: Check the axes: this graph only shows temperature and molecule speed. Pressure isn't on it anywhere, so it can't answer a pressure question. A phase diagram shows temperature AND pressure.

questions.prompt: Landing site Alpha is 20°C with a pressure of 6 atm. What state is water at site Alpha?
questions.why: Find 20°C across and 6 atm up. They meet in the liquid region.

questions.prompt: At site Alpha (20°C, 6 atm), what are the water molecules doing?
questions.why: Water at site Alpha is a liquid, and liquid particles slide past one another while staying close together.

questions.prompt: Normal air pressure on Earth is 1 atm. According to the diagram, at what temperature does water boil at 1 atm?
questions.why: 1 atm is halfway between the 0 and 2 gridlines. Slide right until you hit the boiling line: 100°C.

questions.prompt: At which landing site do the water molecules have the greatest average kinetic energy?
questions.why: Average kinetic energy follows temperature. 150°C is the hottest site, even though its pressure is low.

questions.prompt: A water sample starts at 20°C and 4 atm. The pressure stays at 4 atm while the probe heats it to 180°C. What happens?
questions.why: At 4 atm, move straight right from 20°C to 180°C. You start in liquid and cross the boiling line into gas.

questions.prompt: Water vapor at 160°C and 2 atm is pumped into a chamber. The temperature stays at 160°C while the pressure rises to 10 atm. What happens?
questions.why: At 160°C, move straight up from 2 atm to 10 atm. You start in gas and cross into liquid. Pressure alone changed the state!

questions.prompt: Select ALL the landing sites where the probe would find liquid water.
questions.why: 20°C/6 atm, 50°C/8 atm, and 100°C/10 atm all land in the liquid region.

questions.prompt: Captain Park claims: "Raising the pressure can turn water vapor into liquid water, even when the temperature doesn't change." Pick the TWO statements that are evidence for her claim.
questions.why: Both show the SAME temperature, with a higher pressure causing a change from gas to liquid.

questions.prompt: Look at the pressure axis. What pressure is at the triple point, where solid, liquid, and gas meet?
questions.why: Start at the 1 atm line and count up: the unlabeled lines mean 2, 3, 4, 5... The triple point sits at about 5 atm.

questions.prompt: Mack stores dry ice at normal air pressure, 1 atm, at -100°C. What state is the carbon dioxide?
questions.why: Find -100°C across and 1 atm up. They meet in the solid region.

questions.prompt: On stage, the dry ice stays at 1 atm while it warms from -100°C up to room temperature, 20°C. What happens to it?
questions.why: At 1 atm, move straight right. You go from solid directly into gas. The line at 1 atm never passes through the liquid region!

questions.prompt: What is the name for the change you just traced, when a solid turns directly into a gas?
questions.why: Sublimation is solid straight to gas, skipping the liquid. That's why dry ice never leaves a puddle.

questions.prompt: Mack wonders if CO2 can ever be a liquid. Pick the TWO conditions where carbon dioxide is a liquid.
questions.why: -40°C/20 atm and 0°C/50 atm both land in the liquid region. Liquid CO2 needs a lot of pressure: more than 5 atm!

questions.prompt: At which condition do carbon dioxide molecules have the greatest average kinetic energy?
questions.why: 10°C is the highest temperature on the list, so it has the greatest average kinetic energy, even at a low pressure.

questions.prompt: Once the dry ice has turned into gas on stage, what are the carbon dioxide particles doing?
questions.why: Gas particles move freely and spread far apart, which is why the CO2 spreads across the stage floor.

questions.prompt: What was the air pressure inside the ball at 20°C?
questions.why: Find the 20°C row, then slide across to the pressure column: 8.0 psi.

questions.prompt: About how much higher did the ball bounce at 40°C than at 0°C?
questions.why: The 40°C bar is about 138 cm and the 0°C bar is about 108 cm: a difference of about 30 cm.

questions.prompt: Why did the air pressure inside the ball go up as the ball warmed?
questions.why: Warmer air particles move faster, so they hit the inside of the ball harder and more often. More hits = more pressure.

questions.prompt: Priya left the 60°C row blank. Pick the TWO predictions that fit the pattern in her data.
questions.why: Pressure went up 1.5 psi every 20°C, so about 11 psi at 60°C. Bounce height kept rising, so higher than 138 cm.

questions.prompt: Claim: "The ball bounces higher when it is warmer." Select ALL the evidence that supports the claim.
questions.why: Both statements come straight from the data and show bounce rising with temperature.

questions.prompt: Priya pumps more air into a ball without changing its temperature. What happens inside?
questions.why: More particles in the same space means more collisions with the walls, so the pressure rises.

questions.prompt: A pump can squeeze lots of extra air into a basketball, but you can't squeeze extra water into a full water bottle. Why?
questions.why: Gas particles have lots of empty space between them. Liquid particles are already close together, so there's no room to squeeze.

questions.prompt: Four sealed containers hold the same gas. In which container do the particles have the greatest average kinetic energy?
questions.why: The hottest container wins. Temperature measures average kinetic energy; pressure doesn't.

questions.prompt: Tank A holds air at 10°C and 20 atm. Tank B holds air at 60°C and 2 atm. Which tank's particles have more average kinetic energy?
questions.why: Tank B is hotter, so its particles have more average kinetic energy. The high pressure in Tank A doesn't change that.

questions.prompt: In which state do particles vibrate in place but NOT move past each other?
questions.why: Solid particles are locked in position. They vibrate but don't slide or spread out.

questions.prompt: Juice is poured into a cup. What are the juice particles doing?
questions.why: Juice is a liquid: its particles stay close together but slide past one another, so it can flow.

questions.prompt: A block of ice sits in a freezer at -10°C. What are its water molecules doing?
questions.why: Frozen doesn't mean stopped. Ice molecules vibrate in place.

questions.prompt: A pot of water is heated from 30°C to 70°C. What happens to its molecules?
questions.why: Adding thermal energy speeds particles up.

questions.prompt: Which graph would best answer: "Is carbon dioxide a solid, liquid, or gas at -60°C and 5 atm?"
questions.why: A question about state at a temperature AND a pressure needs a phase diagram.

questions.prompt: Claim: "Ice melts faster in a warm room." Which statement is evidence for this claim?
questions.why: It's true AND it compares warm vs. cool rooms, which is exactly what the claim is about.

questions.prompt: A balloon is carried from a hot car into a cold house, and it shrinks. What happened to the air particles inside?
questions.why: The particles themselves didn't change. They slowed down and moved closer together.

questions.prompt: A sealed jar of air is warmed. Why does the pressure inside go up?
questions.why: Faster particles hit the jar's walls harder and more often. That's what pressure is.

questions.prompt: A small tank for a camping stove holds a LOT of gas. How is that possible?
questions.why: Gas particles have lots of empty space between them, so they can be pushed much closer together.

questions.prompt: A pool float goes a little flat on a chilly night. Which answer explains it using particles?
questions.why: A particle explanation talks about the particles: here, the air particles slowed down and moved closer together.

questions.prompt: You hold an ice cube and your hand feels cold. What is happening?
questions.why: Thermal energy moves from warmer to cooler: out of your hand and into the ice.

questions.prompt: A hand-warmer packet gets hot when you open it. Which statement is true?
questions.why: A hand warmer releases thermal energy, which flows into your cooler hands.

questions.prompt: Frost forms on a window when water vapor turns directly into ice. What is this change called?
questions.why: Gas straight to solid is deposition, the reverse of sublimation.

questions.prompt: At 0°C and 1 atm, ice turns into liquid water. What is this change called?
questions.why: Solid to liquid is melting. (Liquid to solid is freezing.)

questions.prompt: Maya wants to know if fertilizer helps bean plants grow taller. Which plan is a fair test?
questions.why: Only the fertilizer changes. Light and water stay the same, so any difference in height comes from the fertilizer.

questions.prompt: Jamal is testing which brand of paper towel soaks up the most water. What must he keep the same?
questions.why: Only the brand changes. The towel size and the amount of water stay the same, so the test is fair.

questions.prompt: A class is testing whether salt makes ice melt faster. Which setup includes a control?
questions.why: The ice cube with no salt is the control. It shows how fast ice melts anyway, so you can see what the salt really did.

questions.prompt: Ava rolled a toy car down a ramp once and timed it: 4.2 seconds. How can she make her result more trustworthy?
questions.why: Repeating the test and averaging shows whether 4.2 seconds was typical or a fluke.

questions.prompt: Which ice pack keeps a lunch coldest for 4 hours? What should you measure?
questions.why: The question is about how cold the lunch stays over time, so measure the temperature with a thermometer every hour.

questions.prompt: A school needs a water bottle that holds at least 500 mL and costs under $10. Which bottle should it buy?
questions.why: Bottle B is the only one that meets both rules. Bottle A holds the most but costs too much; Bottle C is cheapest but holds too little.

tags.title: Scale Drift Detected
tags.explain: Your instruments are reading off! Before you read a value, find out what each gridline is worth: pick two labeled numbers next to each other on the axis and find the difference. A point between gridlines is between those values, so estimate how far between.
tags.teacherNote: Misread the axis interval, or snapped a between-gridline point to the nearest line.

tags.title: Crossed Wires
tags.explain: Every point has two numbers: one across the bottom (the x-axis) and one up the side (the y-axis). First find the axis whose label matches what the question asks for. Then read your answer from THAT axis.
tags.teacherNote: Answered with the x-value when the y-value was asked (or the reverse).

tags.title: Which Variable Goes Where
tags.explain: The x-axis (along the bottom) gets the variable the scientists CHOSE or changed on purpose, like the temperatures they set or the times they checked. The y-axis (up the side) gets what they MEASURED as a result. Chose it: x-axis. Measured it: y-axis.
tags.teacherNote: Put the measured (dependent) variable on the x-axis. Lesson 5, Step 1.

tags.title: Wrong Target
tags.explain: You read a real value, just not the one the question asked about. Find the question's value on its axis first, put your finger there, then move straight to the line or bar.
tags.teacherNote: Read a neighboring data point instead of the requested one.

tags.title: Uneven Ground
tags.explain: Data points aren't always the same distance apart. A long stretch of line isn't the same as a steep one. To compare, figure out how much the line rises for each step across: rise divided by the distance across.
tags.teacherNote: Judged the size of a change by how long the segment is; ignored uneven x-intervals. Also fires when plotting uneven data at even spacing.

tags.title: Zoom Out
tags.explain: A trend is the overall direction of the whole line from left to right. Ignore the small wiggles. Compare the first point to the last one: the line mostly goes up, mostly goes down, stays flat, or goes up and then down.
tags.teacherNote: Misdescribed the overall direction, or let one segment override the whole pattern.

tags.title: Follow the Path
tags.explain: To predict past the end of the data, keep the line going the way it's already going, including whether it's getting steeper or flatter near the end.
tags.teacherNote: Extrapolated from the wrong part of the curve (e.g., used the early steep slope).

tags.title: Lost the Map
tags.explain: On a phase diagram, find the temperature on the x-axis and the pressure on the y-axis, then slide both until they meet. The region where they meet tells you the state.
tags.teacherNote: Located the (T, P) point in the wrong region.

tags.title: Retrace the Route
tags.explain: When one thing stays the same, you travel in a straight line. Same pressure: move left or right. Same temperature: move up or down. Note the region where you start, then watch for every line you cross.
tags.teacherNote: Traced a change in the wrong direction, or missed crossing a boundary.

tags.title: The Stretchy Ruler
tags.explain: On a log scale, each labeled line is 10 times the one below it: 0.1, 1, 10, 100. The unlabeled lines between two labels count up by the lower label. Between 1 and 10 they mean 2, 3, 4... 9, and they get squeezed closer together near the top. Count lines instead of measuring distance.
tags.teacherNote: Read a log axis as if it were evenly spaced. Tested on the unit test's nitrogen diagram; not practiced in Lesson 5.

tags.title: Row and Column Check
tags.explain: Find the row for the thing you're asked about, then slide across to the right column. Check the column header twice: the cell where your row and column meet is your answer.
tags.teacherNote: Read the wrong row or the wrong column of a data table.

tags.title: Wrong Line
tags.explain: This graph has more than one line. Use the key to find the line for the thing the question asks about (match the shape of its markers), then read only that line.
tags.teacherNote: Read a value or trend from the wrong data series on a multi-line graph.

tags.title: Blueprint Check
tags.explain: A good scale fits ALL the data, counts by the same amount every time, and uses most of the graph so it's easy to read.
tags.teacherNote: Chose a scale that cuts off data, uses unequal intervals, or squashes the data (Lesson 5, Step 2).

tags.title: Temperature Is the Speedometer
tags.explain: Average kinetic energy depends on temperature. Higher temperature means faster particles and more kinetic energy. Pressure can change the state, but it isn't what measures particle energy.
tags.teacherNote: Hanson's named misconception: picking the highest-pressure point for greatest kinetic energy.

tags.title: Know Your States
tags.explain: Solid particles vibrate in place. Liquid particles slide past one another while staying close. Gas particles move freely and spread far apart.
tags.teacherNote: Read the phase correctly but matched it to the wrong particle motion (Hanson's second named misconception).

tags.title: Particles Never Clock Out
tags.explain: Particles in solids, liquids, and gases are always moving. In a solid they vibrate in place, but they never just stop, not even in ice, and not when they're squeezed.
tags.teacherNote: Believes frozen, cold, or high-pressure particles stop moving.

tags.title: Heat Speeds Things Up
tags.explain: Adding thermal energy makes particles move faster. As temperature rises, particle speed rises too. It doesn't hit a limit or turn around.
tags.teacherNote: Believes particle speed plateaus or reverses as temperature rises.

tags.title: Right Tool for the Job
tags.explain: A line graph shows how one thing changes as another changes, like speed vs. temperature. A phase diagram shows which state exists at a temperature AND a pressure. Different questions need different graphs.
tags.teacherNote: Lesson 5's central idea: different graphs answer different questions.

tags.title: Evidence Check
tags.explain: Evidence has to be true AND connected to the claim. A true fact that doesn't show what the claim says isn't evidence for it.
tags.teacherNote: Chose true-but-irrelevant statements as evidence, or missed valid evidence. Supports CER writing.

tags.title: Same Particles, New Moves
tags.explain: Heating, cooling, or squeezing doesn't change the particles themselves. They don't grow, shrink, get heavier, disappear, or break apart. What changes is how fast they move and how far apart they are.
tags.teacherNote: Believes particles themselves grow, shrink, gain mass, break apart, or are destroyed (unit test distractor pattern).

tags.title: Tiny Collisions
tags.explain: Gas pressure comes from particles hitting the walls of their container. More hits, or harder hits, mean more pressure. Faster particles or more particles in the same space both raise the pressure.
tags.teacherNote: Attributes pressure to the weight of gas, suction, or air sneaking in (unit test distractor pattern).

tags.title: Mind the Gap
tags.explain: Gas particles have lots of empty space between them, so they can be squeezed closer together. Liquid and solid particles are already close together, so they barely squeeze at all.
tags.teacherNote: Explains compressibility by weight or particle size instead of spacing.

tags.title: Think Particles
tags.explain: When a question asks what's happening with the particles, the answer has to be about the particles: their speed, their spacing, and their collisions. An explanation about the container or its material doesn't answer the question.
tags.teacherNote: Gave a non-particle explanation (rubber got stiff, can got weak). These are tempting because they sound plausible.

tags.title: Follow the Energy
tags.explain: Cold isn't something that flows. Thermal energy always moves from warmer to cooler. A cold pack feels cold because it absorbs thermal energy from your skin. A hot pack releases thermal energy into it.
tags.teacherNote: Believes 'cold' is transferred, or reverses the direction of thermal energy flow.

tags.title: Name That Change
tags.explain: Melting: solid to liquid. Freezing: liquid to solid. Boiling or evaporation: liquid to gas. Condensation: gas to liquid. Sublimation: solid straight to gas. Deposition: gas straight to solid.
tags.teacherNote: Mixed up phase-change vocabulary or melting point vs. boiling point.

tags.title: One Change at a Time
tags.explain: A fair test changes only ONE thing on purpose: the thing you're trying to find out about. Everything else stays exactly the same. If two things change at once, you can't tell which one caused the result.
tags.teacherNote: Changed more than one variable, or didn't hold the other variables constant (planning investigations).

tags.title: Set Up a Control
tags.explain: A control is a test where you leave out the thing you're testing, like a cup of plain water. It shows what would happen anyway, so you can see how big each real effect is.
tags.teacherNote: Didn't see the need for a control or comparison group.

tags.title: Once Is Never Enough
tags.explain: One result could be a fluke or a mistake. Run every test the same number of times, at least three, then average the results. Repeated trials make your evidence trustworthy.
tags.teacherNote: Relied on a single trial, or ran unequal trials for different groups.

tags.title: Measure What Matters
tags.explain: Measure the thing the question is about, with a tool, at the times that matter. If the client's rules are about temperature at certain times, you need a thermometer reading at those times, not a guess or a feeling.
tags.teacherNote: Chose a measurement that doesn't answer the question (end-only, by feel, or off-target).

tags.title: Check Every Rule
tags.explain: The best choice has to meet ALL of the client's rules. First cross out anything that breaks a rule. Then compare what's left, for example by cost. The most extreme result isn't automatically the best one.
tags.teacherNote: Picked the most extreme or the cheapest option without checking every criterion. Hanson's point: coldest isn't automatically best.
